title: How does your heart move blood?
answer: Put a hand over your chest and you may feel your heart beating. Each beat is a squeeze from a muscle about the size of your fist. The right side sends blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends that blood out to the rest of your body. Each side has a room where blood arrives and another room that pushes blood out. Small flaps called valves open and close so the blood keeps moving in the right direction.

sections.heading: Two trips, one pump
sections.text: Blood returning from the body takes a short trip through the lungs, then comes back to the heart for the trip around the body.

facts: The heart has four chambers.

title: How do lungs get oxygen into your body?
answer: When you breathe in, air travels down your windpipe and through branches that get smaller and smaller inside your lungs. At the ends of many branches are clusters of tiny air sacs. Oxygen from the air passes through the thin walls of those sacs and into the blood. A gas called carbon dioxide moves the other way, from blood into the sacs. When you breathe out, some of that carbon dioxide leaves your body. Your heart keeps sending blood past the sacs so it can pick up oxygen.

sections.heading: The muscle underneath
sections.text: A broad muscle called the diaphragm moves down when it tightens, making more room in your chest so air flows into the lungs.

facts: The tiny air sacs are called alveoli.
The left lung is a little smaller than the right, leaving room for the heart.

title: Where does food go after you swallow it?
answer: Digestion begins before you swallow. Your teeth break up food, and saliva starts breaking down some of it. After you swallow, muscles squeeze food down a tube to your stomach. There it gets churned together with digestive juices. The mixture then moves into your small intestine. There, more juices break food into tiny pieces your body can use, and most nutrients pass out through the intestine wall. Your large intestine takes up water from what is left, and some of the leftovers eventually leave your body as poop.

sections.heading: Food moves even when you lie down
sections.text: Muscles in the wall of the food tube squeeze in waves. This helps push swallowed food along, even when gravity is not pulling it straight down.

facts: The food tube is called the esophagus.
Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.

title: What do your kidneys do?
answer: Your kidneys help keep the right mix of water, salts, and other materials in your blood. Inside each kidney, tiny filters take some water and small materials out of blood. The kidneys then send much of the water and useful materials back. Extra water and some waste leave the kidneys as urine. Thin tubes carry urine to the bladder, where it stays until you pee. These filters work all day, even when you are sleeping or thinking about something else.

sections.heading: A filter plus a return trip
sections.text: A nephron is one of the kidney’s tiny working units. It includes a filter and a tube that gives the body a chance to take back useful material.

facts: Most people have two kidneys.
A healthy kidney has about a million nephrons.

title: How does your brain send messages?
answer: Reaching for a pencil starts with messages traveling between nerve cells. A nerve cell is called a neuron. Electrical signals travel along a neuron, and chemical messengers can pass information across tiny gaps to other cells. Signals from your eyes help your brain work out where the pencil is. Signals from your brain and spinal cord help tell your arm and hand muscles how to move. Neurons also take part in things such as remembering a story or hearing a friend say your name.

sections.heading: Parts have different jobs
sections.text: Areas near the back of your brain help make sense of what you see. Other areas help plan movement, process sound, or remember what happened.

facts: The spinal cord carries many messages between the brain and body.
Your brain does jobs you do not have to think about, including helping control your breathing.

title: How do your ears hear?
answer: A sound sends vibrations through the air. When those vibrations reach your ear, they make a thin part called the eardrum move. Three tiny bones carry the movement farther into the ear. It makes waves in liquid inside the cochlea, a spiral-shaped part of the inner ear. Tiny hair cells respond to this motion and help turn it into signals. A nerve carries those signals to your brain. Your brain makes sense of them as sounds, such as a dog barking or a bell ringing.

sections.heading: Different pitches
sections.text: Different parts of the cochlea respond especially well to different pitches, from a deep drum to a high whistle.

facts: The three tiny bones are in the middle ear.

title: How do muscles move your bones?
answer: When you bend your elbow, muscles near your upper arm put a pull on your bones. Strong strips called tendons attach many muscles to bones. A muscle can shorten and pull, a bit like someone tugging a rope. It cannot push the bone back the other way. To straighten your elbow, a muscle toward the back of your upper arm can pull in another direction. Muscles throughout your body work together to help you stand upright, pick things up, and move without toppling over.

title: What does a fraction tell you?
answer: A fraction can tell you how much of a whole you have. Cut a sandwich into four equal parts. One part is one fourth, written 1/4. The bottom number, 4, tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number, 1, tells how many of those parts you are counting. With three parts, you have 3/4. Fractions can also describe amounts bigger than one whole. Five fourths of a sandwich means a whole sandwich and one extra fourth, if the sandwiches are the same size.

title: How can 1/2 and 2/4 be equal?
answer: Draw two strips of the same length. Divide one into two equal parts and shade one part. Divide the other into four equal parts and shade two parts. Both strips are shaded to exactly the same point. That is why 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent fractions. They describe the same amount using parts of different sizes. On a number line, these two fractions also land at the same spot, halfway between 0 and 1.

title: How do you measure area?
answer: Area tells how much flat space a shape covers. Picture a rectangle made of square tiles that all have the same size. If it has three rows with four tiles in each row, it covers twelve square units. You can count each tile or multiply three by four. This works when the squares fill the shape with no gaps or overlaps. Area measures the inside of a shape. If you instead measured all the way around its edge, you would be finding its perimeter.

title: Why do computers use 0s and 1s?
answer: A computer can store a tiny piece of information in one of two states. We give those states the names 0 and 1. One such choice is called a bit. Put bits together and you can make patterns. A set of agreed rules can tell a computer which pattern stands for a letter, a number, or a color. Binary numbers use only 0 and 1. Their places count in ones, twos, fours, eights, and so on, each place worth twice as much as the one to its right.

title: What is an algorithm?
answer: An algorithm is a set of steps for solving a problem or doing a job. Imagine looking for your name in a list that is sorted from A to Z. One plan is to start at the top and read each name in order. Another is to start near the middle and decide which half to keep looking in. Both can find your name, but the second plan can save time on a long sorted list. Computers can follow algorithms when each step is clear enough for them to carry it out.

sections.heading: A useful rule can have a condition

title: What is phishing?
answer: Phishing is a trick where someone makes a message look trustworthy to get you to give them something or do something. They might ask for a password, send a link that leads to a fake sign-in page, or try to get you to open a file. Some messages pretend to be from a familiar game or website. If a message surprises you or asks you to rush, stop before you tap anything. Show it to a trusted grown-up who can help check where it came from.

title: Why do you need a password?
answer: A password is a secret you enter to help show you are allowed to sign in to an account. If someone else learns it, they may be able to sign in as you. A long password that is hard to guess helps protect the account. Using a different one on each account helps too. Then learning one password does not give someone the same secret for all your accounts. If you are setting up an account, a trusted grown-up can help you choose a password and a safe way to keep it.

title: How does a lever make a job easier?
answer: A lever is a stiff piece that turns around a fixed point. A seesaw is a lever, and the support under its middle is the turning point, called a fulcrum. If you push down on one end, the other end goes up. Moving the turning point closer to the thing you want to lift can make the lift take less force. In return, the end you push has to move farther than the object rises. The same trade can help a crowbar lift a heavy lid.

sections.heading: Try it with a ruler

facts: A fulcrum is the point about which a lever turns.

title: How does a pulley help lift something?
answer: A pulley is a wheel with a groove that guides a rope or cable. Hang one pulley from a support, run a rope over it, and tie a load to one end. You can pull down on the other end to make the load rise. That single fixed pulley changes the direction of your pull. Using more pulleys in a different arrangement can also make a big load easier to lift. The trade is that you have to pull a longer stretch of rope to raise the load the same distance.

facts: A fixed pulley can change the direction of a pull.
